Dear one, may you not beget such vile men, who abandon their helpers in battle and go home in safety.
mahabharata:12:98.21	The gods led by Indra work ill for them: he who wishes to save his own life by abandoning his helpers,
mahabharata:12:98.22	they should kill with sticks and clods, or burn in a fire of straw, or slay like an animal—such kshatriyas as these.
mahabharata:12:98.23	This is unrighteous for a kshatriya, that he should die on a bed, discharging phlegm and bile, lamenting piteously.
mahabharata:12:98.24	The kshatriya who meets his end with an unwounded body—the ancient sages do not praise that deed of his.
mahabharata:12:98.25	Death at home is not praised for kshatriyas, dear one; for the heroic it is unheroic, unrighteous and pitiable.
mahabharata:12:98.26	This is sorrow, oh, this is misery, this is worse," he groans, his face distorted, foul, grieving greatly for his ministers.
He envies the healthy and even longs for death again and again; a hero, proud and self-respecting, does not deserve such a death.
Having wrought slaughter in battles, surrounded by kinsmen, sorely hurt by sharp weapons, the kshatriya deserves death.
For the hero, filled with truth and anger, fights fiercely; his limbs being cut by the enemy, he does not even notice.
Meeting death in battle, praised and honoured by the world, having attained his own great dharma, he goes to Shakra's world.
Every warrior, possessed with the resolve to give up his life, attains Indra's world, the hero who never shows his back."
On this too they recite this ancient history, Yudhishthira—the conversation of Ambarisha and Indra.
Ambarisha, son of Nabhaga, having gone to heaven so hard to reach, saw his own general, the lord, together with Shakra in the world of the gods,
seated in a splendid divine aerial car, all radiant, going higher and higher.
Seeing the general going above him, the high-minded one, astonished at Sudeva's prosperity, spoke to Vasava:

Having ruled the whole earth to its ocean boundary according to rule, I acted among the four classes according to the scriptures, desiring dharma.
mahabharata:12:99.7	By fierce celibacy and service to my teacher's household, having studied the Vedas in dharma and the science of kings alone,
mahabharata:12:99.8	with food and drink for guests, with offerings for the ancestors, with study and vows for the sages, with the highest sacrifices for the gods,
mahabharata:12:99.9	established in kshatriya dharma, according to scripture and rule, I conquered armies in battle, Vasava, looking on them.
mahabharata:12:99.15	The officiating priests were elephants there, the adhvaryus horses; the oblations were flesh, and blood was the ghee.
mahabharata:12:99.16	Jackals, vultures and crows were the assembly-members and sacrificers there; they drink the remains of the ghee and eat the offering at the rite.
mahabharata:12:99.17	Heaps of lances and javelins, swords, spears and axes, blazing, sharp, and drinking, were his ladles, and then the sacrificers.
mahabharata:12:99.18	An arrow, drawn by the bow's force, sharp, piercing the enemy's body, straight, well whetted and drinking, is his great ladle.
mahabharata:12:99.19	A sword bound in leopard hide, with a hilt made of elephant's tusk, held in the elephant's trunk, is his spatula in battle.
mahabharata:12:99.20	With blazing, sharp, drinking lances, spears and axes, with iron-made darts, a sharp blow would be the wealth.
mahabharata:12:99.21	The blood that flows in battle from the rush upon the ground is his full oblation, rich for the hotri, granting all desires.
mahabharata:12:99.22	He in whose van it is heard Cut! Split!"—the Sama singers sing the Samas of that man in Yama's abode.
The enemies' van is called his oblation-shed; the heap of elephants, horses and armoured men is, they say, the fire called Shyenachit, which is arranged at his sacrifice.
A headless trunk rises there when a thousand are slain; that is the sacrificial post of that hero, of khadira wood, eight-cornered, it is said.
Elephants driven by goads cry out the Ida invocation; with the din of the bowstring and the vashat-call, O king, in your battle the Udgatri is the three-fold sama, and the drum is remembered.
He who, when a Brahmana's wealth is being seized, gives up his dear body in battle, raising himself as the sacrificial post, his sacrifice has endless fees.
The hero who strikes in the van for his master's sake and does not turn back from fear, his worlds are like mine.
He for whom the altar is spread with swords like dark crescent moons and arms like iron clubs, his worlds are like mine.
He who, standing in victory, looks to no helper at all, plunging into the midst of the army, his worlds are like mine.
He for whom the masses of lances are the drum, frogs and tortoises, the heroes' bones the gravel, difficult the mud of flesh and blood,
the river with swords and shields for rafts, with hair for moss and grass, bridged by horses, elephants and chariots broken,
with banners and standards for reeds, with slain mounts as its army, full of flowing blood, hard to cross for men who would cross,
with slain elephants for great crocodiles, bearing to the other world, inauspicious, with spears, swords and flags for its boats, with vultures, herons and ducks for rafts,
haunted by flesh-eaters, bringing faintness to cowards—that river is the concluding bath at the warrior's great sacrifice.
He whose altar is strewn with the heads of his enemies, with horses' shoulders and elephants' shoulders, his worlds are like mine.
He who has made the enemy's van his wife's hall, and his own army the oblation-shed, the wise say that is his rite.
The assembly-hall and, within, the warrior-fire, and the Agnidhra to the north—the enemy host as his wife—all worlds are not far from him.
When on both sides the cry is raised and the sky is before him, that is his altar in the sacrifice; the three Vedas and fires are ever there.
The warrior who turns away, terrified, and is slain by the enemy, goes to a hell without foothold; there is no doubt in this.
He for whom a river is flooded by the force of blood, mixed with hair, flesh and bones, goes to the highest goal.
He who, having slain the general, mounts his vehicle, has the stride of Vishnu, a sacrifice equal to Brihaspati.
He who seizes alive a leader or a measure of authority, or one honoured there, his worlds are like mine.
One should never grieve for a hero slain in battle; the slain hero is not to be grieved for, and is exalted in heaven.
No food or water, no bath nor impurity, they wish to do for him who is slain; hear from me his worlds.
Thousands of excellent apsarases run hurrying to the hero slain in the fight, saying, "Let him be my husband."
This is austerity and merit and eternal dharma, and the four stages of life belong to him who does not flee in battle.
One should not slay the old, a child, nor a woman, nor a Brahmana, nor one who says "I am yours" with grass in his mouth.
I slew Vritra, Bala, Paka, Shatamaya, Virochana, the unstoppable Namuchi, and Shambara of many illusions,
Vipraichitti the Daitya, the sons of Danu in every way, and Prahlada, in battle, and then I became lord of the gods."
Hearing and accepting this speech of Shakra, Ambarisha attained the accomplishment of warriors for himself.
Janaka of Mithila, wearing the sacred thread in battle, roused the warriors; hear that, Yudhishthira.
Janaka, king of Mithila, the great-souled knower of all truths, showed his own warriors heaven and hell alike.

These shining worlds are for the fearless—behold!—full of Gandharva maidens, yielding all desires, imperishable.
mahabharata:12:100.5	These hells await those who flee, and lasting infamy, and a fall straight after.
mahabharata:12:100.6	Seeing them, conquer the foe, with minds resolved to renounce; do not come under the sway of the hell without foothold.
Renunciation is the root for heroes, the highest door to heaven—thus the king told those warriors, scourge of foes,
and they conquered their enemies in battle, gladdening the lord of men. Therefore the self-controlled man should always stand at the head of battle.
Chariot-warriors in the midst of elephants, horsemen behind the chariots, and between the horsemen the armoured footmen should be stationed.
The king who arrays thus always conquers his foes; therefore, Yudhishthira, it should always be done so.
All, desiring merit and very wrathful in good fighting, should shake the enemy ranks as sea-monsters churn the ocean.
They should cheer the despondent, arranging one another, and guard the conquered ground; one should not pursue the broken.
The onrush of those turning back and hopeless of life is not easy to bear, O king; therefore one should not pursue.
For heroes do not wish to strike those fleeing in fear; therefore let there be no pursuit of the fleeing.
The immobile are food of the mobile, the fangless of the fanged, the handless of the handed; the cowards are food of the hero.
With the same back, belly, hands and feet, the cowards follow the hero from behind; then, stricken with fear, bowing again, with joined palms they wait on the heroes.
This world hangs on the hero's arms like a son always; therefore in all conditions the hero deserves honour.
There is nothing higher than heroism in the three worlds; the hero protects all; everything is established in the hero."

Dharmas are established by truth, others by reasoning, some by good conduct, and others are expedient. I shall tell the expedient dharmas that accomplish the aims of wealth and dharma.
mahabharata:12:101.3	Robbers who are without restraint become obstructors; to counter them I shall now tell the rule. Learn from me those means for the success of tasks.
mahabharata:12:101.4	There are two kinds of wisdom to be known, straight and crooked, Bharata; knowing the crooked, one should not practise it but should resist it when it comes.
mahabharata:12:101.5	Enemies approach a king by sowing division; the king, knowing that deceit, should afflict the enemies accordingly.
mahabharata:12:101.6	Side-hides of elephants, and of bulls, cows and pythons, and iron plates, are held to be armour.
mahabharata:12:101.7	Weapons should be whetted and polished; armours yellow and red; the banners and flags should be coloured with many dyes.
mahabharata:12:101.8	Lances, javelins, swords, sharp axes, shields and hides should be prepared in multiples; weapons should be brought up and the warriors rested.
mahabharata:12:101.9	In Chaitra or Margashirsha the marshalling of the army is praised, for then the earth is ripe with crops and has water.
mahabharata:12:101.11	A road with water and grass, level and passable, is praised; for it has been practised by skilled spies who range the forests.
mahabharata:12:101.12	It could not be traversed by new forest herds as by bands of deer; therefore those who seek victory employ it in all armies.
mahabharata:12:101.13	A camp with water and a fort, with open space, is praised; and there should be a defence against the approach of enemies.
mahabharata:12:101.14	Open ground near a forest they consider more advantageous, those people skilled in war, for its many sorts of merits.
mahabharata:12:101.15	Planting oneself, retreating, concealing the footmen, then repelling the foe, and a refuge for calamity.
mahabharata:12:101.16	Placing the seven sages behind them, they should fight unmoving as mountains; by this rule, O king, one may seek to conquer even the hard to conquer.
mahabharata:12:101.17	Where the wind is, where the sun is, where Shukra is, there is victory; each earlier is better for victory when they meet, Yudhishthira.
mahabharata:12:101.18	Ground without mud, without water, without boundaries, without clods is praised for horses by people skilled in war.
mahabharata:12:101.19	Level ground without water and open sky is praised as chariot-ground; ground with low trees, great thickets and water is for elephant-warriors.
mahabharata:12:101.20	Ground with many forts, great trees, spread with canes and bamboos, and mountains and groves, is fit for footmen.
mahabharata:12:101.21	An army abundant in footmen is firm, Bharata; one abundant in chariots and horses is praised in fine weather.
mahabharata:12:101.22	One abundant in footmen and elephants is praised in the rainy season; weighing these merits, one should employ place and time.
mahabharata:12:101.23	He who goes thus, having reflected, honoured by lunar day and star, always wins victory, deploying his army rightly.
mahabharata:12:101.24	One should not strike the sleeping, thirsty, weary or scattered, nor at release, at marching, at moving, nor at drinking and eating time.
mahabharata:12:101.25	Those thrown into disorder, scattered, shattered, thinned, those greatly trusting and who have begun a work, those harassing by ambush, the roaming outside, those who return to their houses after setting ambush...
mahabharata:12:101.26	At the gate come down through succession, any who follow, the attendants, the guards, and any boasters,
mahabharata:12:101.27	those who break the ranks and those who hold the broken together, who share food and drink, should be given double pay.
mahabharata:12:101.28	Commanders of ten should be made, and of a hundred; over them one should make a commander of a thousand, a hero and untiring.
mahabharata:12:101.29	Assembling them according to rank, they should be told: We swear that, for victory, we shall not abandon one another in battle.
Let those who are cowards among us turn back here; let them not, making a breach in the tumult, cause us to be slain.
Fleeing, one slays himself and his own side in battle; loss of goods, death, infamy and disgrace are in flight.
Pleasing and unpleasant are the words of a man who flees, with trembling lips and teeth, with all weapons laid down.
May it be so for our enemies: one who, abandoning his helpers when life is in doubt, flees, pursued by foes.
Those who turn away are the dregs of men; they merely swell the count; they are nothing here nor hereafter.
Enemies with glad minds go out to meet the fleer; the friends of the victor, dear one, greet with salutations and blessings.
That which enemies delight in at a man's misfortune, O king, I think a sorrow more unbearable even than death.
Know Fortune to be the root of dharma and of all happiness; she departs from cowards, and the hero wins her.
So we, desiring heaven, having given up life in battle, whether conquering or slain, deserve to reach a good goal."
Thus, with oaths sworn and life abandoned, the fearless heroes plunge into the enemy host.
In front should be the line of men with swords and shields, behind the line of wagons, and the women in the middle.
To counter the enemy, and to conceal the footmen, those in the van should be eager for the foe.
Those who are esteemed in front, the courageous and spirited, should advance first, and the other men follow them.
Even the cowards should be encouraged with effort; let them merely show their shoulders or stay near.
A few should be made to fight massed together; the many may be spread as desired; the needle-faced array is for few with many.
In the clash, or when elated, truly or falsely, raising their arms, they should cry: "The foe are broken, broken!"
Our friends' force has come; strike fearlessly! they should run after them shouting, making a dreadful roar.
They should sound shouts and howls, conches, saws, cow-horns, kettledrums, mridangas and tabors, and make the elephants trumpet.
[Bhishma said:] "The writ of arms is ordained according to conduct; a man acts in deeds according to his behaviour.
The Gandharas, Sindhu-Sauviras, fighters with claws and lances, the Abhiras, are strong; that force goes through everything.
The Ushinaras are skilled in all weapons and brave; the Easterners are skilled in elephant fighting and fight by craft.
So too the Yavanas, Kambojas, and those around Mathura; these are skilled in wrestling; the Southerners carry swords and shields.
Heroes are born everywhere, of great spirit and strength; this is mostly stated; hear now the marks from me.
With eyes like lions and tigers, and the gait of lions and tigers, with eyes like pigeons and lapwings, all are heroes, crushers.
Some with voices of deer, eyes of leopards, or eyes of bulls, are loud talkers, very fierce and wrathful, with kinnara voices.
Some with voices of clouds, angry faces, voices like young camels, with crooked noses and calves, going far and hitting far.
Some are like cats and hunchbacks, thin, with thin hair and thin skin, heroes and fickle-minded, hard to approach.
Some with eyes closed like iguanas, and gentle in nature, with the sound of a horse's gait—those men are able to carry through.
Well knit, lean, broad-chested, well set, they dance and rejoice at music and in quarrels.
With deep eyes, protruding eyes, tawny, with frowning faces, with eyes like mongooses—all these are heroes who give up life.
With squinting eyes and broad foreheads, with fleshless jaws, with crooked arms and fingers, thin, with veins stretched,
they rush in with great speed when the battle is at hand; like maddened elephants they are hard to approach.
With hair-ends bright and bursting, broad flanks, jaws and faces, high shoulders, thick necks, fearsome, with thick calves,
upright with fine necks, bent like birds, with heads like balls, with serpent faces and mouths like bulls' bites,
with fierce voices, wrathful, rushing with roars in battles, ignorant of dharma and arrogant, terrible, showing savagery,
all these have abandoned themselves, are of low birth and do not turn back; they should always be put in the van of the army; they are slain and they slay.
They are unrighteous and of broken conduct; their defeat is well; just so they are constantly enraged even at kings."
[Bhishma said:] "I shall tell you in full, bull among men, the forms that are auspicious in an army that is to win.
Fate works first, when human effort is driven by time; the learned see that with eyes lengthened by knowledge.
They know here the rule of expiation, muttering and oblations; doing auspicious rites they pacify even the evil omens.
The army in which the warriors and mounts are high-spirited, Bharata, one should say victory is certain for it.
When winds blow behind it, and rainbows, and clouds and the sun's rays follow it,
when jackals, mares and vultures move on every side favourably around the army, then success is supreme.
A fire with bright radiance, with rays upward, with flame turning to the right, smokeless, and sweet scents of the oblations blowing—they call this the form of coming victory.
Where conches and kettledrums resound deep and loud, and the eager are unopposed—they call this the form of coming victory.
Where birds speak auspicious sounds, swans, cranes, hundred-petal birds and chasha birds, and the spirited warriors are glad—they call this the form of coming victory.
With weapons, cloaks, armours, banners, fine rays and bright faces of the young, the army is dazzling and hard to look at; those whose host it is overcome their enemies.
Where the warriors are obedient, free of pride, bound in friendship with one another, and practise purity—they call this the form of coming victory.
Sounds, touches and scents pleasing to the mind move about, and steadiness enters the warriors; that is the face of victory.
The left is favourable for one entering, the right for one wishing to enter; behind it accomplishes the aim, in front it prevents.
Having gathered a great fourfold army, Yudhishthira, one should first try in battle to turn it back by conciliation alone.
This victory is the lowest, namely war, Bharata; in battle victory is a matter of chance or fate, so it is considered.
Like the great surge of waters, like frightened herds of deer, a great army once broken is hardest to check.
They are broken just because "they are broken"; even the learned are not the cause; a great army of fine strength is like a herd of ruru deer.
Even fifty heroes who know one another, glad, resolved to give up life, firmly determined, crush the enemy host.
Or five, six or seven united, resolved, well-born and well honoured, conquer their enemies here.
One should never go to a clash when it is possible otherwise; conciliation, division and gifts—war is said to be last.
By the advance of an army fear afflicts the cowards; where will this fall, like a blazing thunderbolt?
Knowing that a force has set out, those who go out against it—the limbs of the warriors and of the country quiver.
The whole country trembles, O king, with its fixed and moving things; the marrow of embodied beings scorched by the heat of weapons sinks.
To them conciliation mixed with harshness should be applied again and again; for pressed on all sides, enemies come to terms.
To split the intermediaries he should send spies, and with the king who is beyond him a treaty is praised.
For no other way can torment him so as does obstructing him on all sides together with an enemy.
Forbearance is good, yes, a stratagem; non-forbearance is never good; know, Partha, the purpose of forbearance and of non-forbearance.
A king who forbears after conquering increases in fame; even enemies who have greatly offended trust him.
Shambara thought forbearance good after having weakened; but wood that is not heated returns again to its nature.
The teachers do not praise this, nor is it a good example; they should be restrained without distress or destruction, like one's own sons.
A fierce king becomes hated by beings, Yudhishthira; they despise even a mild one; therefore he should be of both kinds.
Even about to strike he should speak pleasantly, Bharata, and having struck he should show compassion, as if grieving, as if weeping.
It is not dear to me that he was slain, he should say, speaking thus before; "you did not do what I said though told again and again."
As a potter makes from a lump of clay whatever he wishes, so a man obtains the deed done by himself.
Oppressed by many, his treasury exhausted and without vehicles, the king with his servants and city fell into great distress.
Seeing the ruin of all the kings, the elder brother of Gada, Janardana, deemed this the highest good.
Hearing her words, Keshava, slayer of heroes, wrathful, cast a sidelong glance with an angry eye.
[Indra said:] "You will see your brothers and sons who have gone to heaven before, all with Krishna; do not grieve, bull of the Bharatas."
What did Duryodhana, son of Dhritarashtra, do, that, endowed with such fortune, that sinner, with all his followers...
